summary: Path Segment Identifiers (PSIDs) identify and correlate bidirectional or end-to-end paths in Segment Routing. This document defines LSP ping procedures for checking SR paths that use a PSID over the MPLS data plane.

eli5.summary: A ping is like shouting to see if someone answers. This explains how to check that a labeled route through the network works from end to end.

questions: what is a path segment identifier
what are psid sub-tlvs in mpls
how is a psid validated by lsp ping
subtitle: Six new LSP Ping sub-TLVs let an operator check that a Path Segment Identifier is set up correctly at the end of a Segment Routing path.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing paths over MPLS can carry a Path Segment Identifier (PSID) that the egress node uses to recognize the path, but LSP Ping had no way to check that a PSID reached the right node and matches what that node was told.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs (types 49 to 54), one for each combination of SR Policy, Candidate Path or Segment List and IPv4 or IPv6. It adds a validation step 4b so the endpoint compares the fields it receives with what it has signaled or provisioned.
tldr.outcome: Operators can verify a PSID against the control plane with LSP Ping. LSP Traceroute is left out because transit nodes do not take part in PSID processing.

today: RFC 9884 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PSIDs Need Their Own Ping
sections.content:
A Path Segment is a local segment (RFC 9545) that uniquely identifies a Segment Routing (SR) path on the egress node. Its Path Segment Identifier (PSID) is a single label taken from the SR Local Block (SRLB) of the egress node, defined in RFC 8402.

The ingress node inserts the PSID as one label immediately after the last label of the SR path in the MPLS label stack. The egress node pops it.

LSP Ping (RFC 8029) can then be used in two ways. It can check that a PSID reached the intended node and was processed correctly. It can also verify the SR path context (segment list, candidate path or SR Policy) tied to the PSID, as signaled or provisioned at the egress node.
sections.eli5: A tag on the last piece of a long trail tells the end of the trail which trail you came along. This document gives us a way to test that the tag is right.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Sub-TLV
sections.content:
Following the style of RFC 8287 and RFC 9703, the RFC defines six new sub-TLVs for the Target FEC Stack TLV (Type 1), the Reverse-Path Target FEC Stack TLV (Type 16) and the Reply Path TLV (Type 21). There are three kinds, each in an IPv4 and an IPv6 form.

A PSID can stand for all segment lists of an SR Policy, all segment lists of one candidate path, or a single segment list. The sender picks the sub-TLV that matches what the PSID identifies:

  • All segment lists in an SR Policy: the SR Policy Associated PSID sub-TLV MUST be used.
  • All segment lists in a candidate path: the SR Candidate Path Associated PSID sub-TLV MUST be used.
  • A single segment list: the SR Segment List Associated PSID sub-TLV MUST be used.
  • Some segment lists in a candidate path or policy: the Segment List sub-TLV is used, and multiple LSP Ping messages MUST be sent, each carrying one such sub-TLV.

These sub-TLVs are not expected to appear together in one message. If several are present, only the first is processed.
sections.eli5: You can name a whole family, one branch of the family, or one single person. There is a different kind of test note for each, so the answerer knows how closely to check.

sections.title: The Sub-TLV Formats
sections.content:
Every sub-TLV starts with a 2-octet Type and a 2-octet Length. Length excludes those first 4 octets and MUST be set to a fixed value for each type.

The Policy sub-TLVs carry a Headend address, a 4-octet Color and an Endpoint address, as defined in RFC 9256. Addresses are 4 octets for IPv4 and 16 octets for IPv6.

The Candidate Path sub-TLVs add a 1-octet Protocol-Origin (from an IANA registry; an unsupported value makes validation at the responder fail), 3 reserved octets (zero on send, ignored on receipt), a 20-octet Originator and a 4-octet Discriminator. The Segment List sub-TLVs add a 4-octet Segment-List-ID, a term this RFC introduces for the identifier of a segment list within a candidate path.
sections.eli5: Each test note is a form. The short form asks for a few names. The longer forms ask more questions, until the longest one points to exactly one trail.

sections.title: How the Endpoint Validates a PSID
sections.content:
An LSP Ping can be started by the headend of the SR path or by a centralized topology-aware data plane monitoring system (RFC 8403). For a PSID, the node that answers the echo request MUST be the endpoint of the SR path.

The endpoint first checks the sub-TLV. A malformed one is answered with return code 1, 'Malformed echo request received'. Otherwise the RFC adds a step 4b, Segment Routing PSID Validation, after step 4a of Section 7.4 of RFC 8287. When the label stack depth is 1, the endpoint checks that the PSID is signaled or provisioned for the policy, candidate path or segment list, and that the received fields match.

  • Policy: headend, color and endpoint.
  • Candidate path: headend, color, endpoint, originator and discriminator.
  • Segment list: those five plus the segment-list-id.

If any check fails, the best return code is 10, 'Mapping for this FEC is not the given label at stack-depth'. If all pass, the return code is 3, 'Replying router is an egress for the FEC at stack-depth', and the FEC-Status is set to 1.
sections.eli5: The person at the end of the trail looks at your note and checks every detail against their own list. If one detail is wrong, they say 'not mine'. If all match, they say 'yes, I am the end of this trail'.

sections.title: Reverse Path and Reply Handling
sections.content:
Any of the six sub-TLVs may be carried in a Reverse-Path Target FEC Stack TLV (Type 16) or a Reply Path TLV (Type 21). When one is, an endpoint MUST send it in an echo reply.

The headend then runs the same validity checks, but without setting the return code. If any validation fails, the headend MUST drop the echo reply and SHOULD log or report an error.

The RFC leaves LSP Traceroute out of scope. Its stated reason is that transit nodes are not involved in PSID processing.
sections.eli5: The answer can carry the same tag back. The sender checks it too, and throws the reply away if something does not match.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The new sub-TLVs follow the mechanisms of RFC 8029, so all the security considerations in Section 5 of that RFC apply. The RFC states that the sub-TLVs do not impose any additional security challenges.

IANA has assigned sub-types 49 to 54 in the 'Sub-TLVs for TLV Types 1, 16, and 21' registry, using the Standards Action range (0-16383) in which an error message must be returned if the sub-TLV is not recognized.
sections.eli5: Because this only adds new kinds of test notes to an existing system, it brings no new danger. The old safety rules still apply.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Sub-TLV length excluding the first 4 octets.

fields.name: Headend
fields.desc: Headend IPv4 address of the SR Policy.

fields.name: Color
fields.desc: Color (policy identifier) of the SR Policy.

fields.name: Endpoint
fields.desc: Endpoint IPv4 address of the SR Policy.

fields.name: Protocol-Origin
fields.desc: Protocol that originated the candidate path.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero when sent, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Originator
fields.desc: Originator of the candidate path (20 octets).

fields.name: Discriminator
fields.desc: Identifies the candidate path within Headend, Color and Endpoint.

fields.name: Segment-List-ID
fields.desc: Identifies the segment list within the candidate path.
